NutSack39
Now you may be wondering why I gave Elden Ring a 0/10 rating. When I first put the game in, I was genuinely amazed. I thought it was awesome. Extraordinary, even. I was like “yeah, this is it, this is peak gaming.” The world looked insane, the combat felt intense, everything was mysterious and cool and I was fully locked in from the start. But then I ran into one small problem that completely ruined my entire experience. I thought there was going to be a powerful, legendary, wearable ring called the Elden Ring. Like an actual ring. Something you equip. Something that gives you insane stats. Something that makes you basically unstoppable and cool-looking at the same time. That’s what I signed up for. So naturally, I started looking for it. At first it was casual. Just exploring. Doing a few fights. Checking the map. “I’ll find it soon,” I thought. But then it escalated. I started clearing entire regions. Killing bosses. Reading item descriptions I didn’t understand. Talking to NPCs like they were going to drop hints. It became personal. And the worst part is—I think I was too far gone to stop. I should’ve paid more attention to the story and the cutscenes, but instead I got locked into this idea that the Elden Ring was somewhere out there, just waiting to be found and equipped. So I kept pushing forward, thinking “it has to be next area, it has to be this boss, it has to be this dungeon.”Hours turned into days. Days turned into way too many hours. And then I finally reached the end of the game. And what do I find? Not a ring. Not even close. Just some giant dumbass yellow tree situation called the Elden Ring or something. At that point I was already in too deep. 300+ hours gone. Fully invested. Emotionally committed. And the “Elden Ring” turns out to be a metaphysical concept tied to a ugly ass yellow tree that you absolutely cannot wear on your finger. And even if it wasn’t broken or whatever… I still can’t wear it. Which feels like a major design oversight, if you ask me. So yeah. That’s why I give this game a 0/10.

Kakaenkyou
FromSoftware's Elden Ring is nothing short of a watershed moment for the medium. Hidetaka Miyazaki and George R. R. Martin have forged a world that feels both impossibly vast and meticulously handcrafted — every windswept plain, crumbling ruin, and fog-laden catacomb whispers a story without ever spelling it out. The Lands Between is not a checklist of icons on a map; it is a place that rewards curiosity with awe, and punishes complacency with grace.

Libi_Aeryn
-no believable world, repetitive gameplay- As a side note: my criticism isn't about difficulty. I was already level 55 with under 15 hours, 83 by 20h (besides exploration - farming soldiers in Gatefront Ruins and militia in Greyoll's Dragonbarrow for fast runes). Finished the game in 80h. The game has positive aspects, but for me the weaknesses clearly outweigh them. The most positive point first: the monster design is magnificent. Many creatures, bosses, and enemies look fantastic and have an impressive presence. I also like the system with the spirit companions. That is already where the strengths end. The world does not feel alive, but artificially pieced together. Instead of a believable fantasy world, I see a collection of enemies, ruins, and loot subjects/objects without meaning or connection. It feels as if everything is only there for grinding. There is hardly any normal life, hardly any society, hardly anything that gives the impression that this world is not just a backdrop for battles. The NPCs are often blurry and also seem placed into the landscape arbitrarily. Right at the beginning, you encounter a merchant who looks like Santa Claus. What is especially disturbing for me is the artificial enemy AI. In some cases, the enemies behave absurdly stupidly. They stand in immediate proximity while you slaughter their comrades. These die screaming loudly, fall to the ground dramatically, and even break entire wooden carts into pieces in the process – yet the other enemies seem to take no notice of it at all. Once an enemy has spotted the player, it is often enough to crouch briefly – no matter whether you are crouching directly in their field of vision! (as long as you maintain a certain distance). Even if you are actually still in direct line of sight, they suddenly lose all interest, turn around, and walk away. If they randomly walk in the same direction as the player, it is usually enough to make a small detour around them, and you can already assassinate them from behind. The progression system also did not convince me. Neither leveling attributes nor upgrading weapons feels particularly noticeable in combat. At the same time, the combat strength of many enemies often seems arbitrary. Instead of a comprehensible increase in power, the impression of an unbalanced system often arises. For this very reason, I do not experience Elden Ring as challenging in the sense of a fair, high difficulty level. Instead, much of it feels unbalanced, inconsistent, and unnecessarily unfriendly to the player. Not to mention the imprecise controls. The game often does not challenge the player through intelligent systems or believable challenges, but rather through idiosyncratic design decisions that create frustration without increasing enjoyment accordingly. On top of that comes the storytelling approach. After many hours, I never had the feeling of following an exciting story. Instead, you run around, collect items, upgrade weapons, level up, and defeat monsters. But for what purpose, actually? The story here is a pale excuse to at least have a bad explanation of what you are supposed to do in this world. The whole game principle ultimately boils down to finding stronger equipment in order to defeat stronger enemies, so that you can find even stronger equipment in order to defeat even stronger enemies. I found this cycle pointless and not very motivating. However, if you are as ambitious as I am, you run the risk of spending hours upon hours farming runes or searching for useful items, not because it is fun, but because you simply want to progress. The rune system sounds interesting on paper: when you die, the runes remain at the place of death. In practice, this mostly just means additional running distances. It gets even more absurd in dungeons. If you jump down a small ledge, there is often no way back. The character can fight gigantic monsters, but cannot climb a chest-high rock. Such limitations do not feel challenging to me, but simply unnatural and unuser-friendly. It is better to always enter a dungeon without runes, because if you are still too weak for the enemies inside (which you cannot know, since in the same regions absurdly weak and absurdly strong enemies coexist), then you might lose all your runes. Graphically, I am also conflicted. The landscapes and monsters can look impressive, but many NPCs and some enemies (knights, wolves) feel stiff, strange, and in some cases noticeably weaker in quality than the creatures. This creates a strange contrast for me between excellent monster design and less convincing character models. Conclusion: Hardly any atmospheric sense of travel, no believable world, repetitive gameplay loop. Technically and artistically impressive in individual areas, but as a gameplay experience for me neither motivating nor satisfying. The beautiful monsters alone are not enough to compensate for the many weaknesses.
